docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
🧬 immunarch – Multi-modal immune repertoire analysis in R

Tutorials | API reference | Ecosystem | Publication (coming soon...)

immunarch brings a comprehensive analytics toolkit to build reproducible analysis pipelines for Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) data with a particular focus on designing personalized immunotherapies and vaccines. Key features are:

  • Multi-modal immune profiling: compute AIRR statistic, combining them with single-cell, spatial, immunogenicity or any other receptor annotations;

  • Immunomics at scale: work seamlessly with datasets that don't fit in memory;

  • Immune biomarker discovery: stratify cohorts and timepoints, derive repertoire signatures (diversity/clonality, V/J usage, similarity), and track antigen-annotated receptors;

  • Feature engineering: build Machine Learning-ready feature tables (receptor-, sample- and cohort-level) from core repertoire metrics and annotations;

  • Modular, extendable, adaptable: add new analyses and metrics via an extension API, and use adapters to interoperate with other AIRR tools and formats.

docs.title: 🤔 Why immunarch?
docs.text:
As immune repertoire sequencing becomes a mainstream technology, adopted by major platforms and integrated into more translational and clinical workflows, tooling expectations are changing rapidly. The pace of both innovation and data growth outstrips what even the most dedicated tool developers can deliver.

That's why it's the perfect moment to step back and rethink how and why we analyze AIRR data. Instead of racing to patch each new problem, we need to prepare for the next epoch of immunomics.

What defines this next epoch?

A massive shift in focus: from pure research towards biomarker discovery, personalized immunotherapies, and integration of immune repertoire data into real clinical decision making.

Today's AIRR analysis must handle:

  • Multi-modal data: bulk and single-cell V(D)J, spatial transcriptomics, gene expression, clinical metadata, and antigen specificity -- all together;

  • Massive scale: experiments that move from gigabytes to tens or hundreds of gigabytes, or even terabytes;

  • Reproducibility and collaboration: workflows that need to be shared, versioned, and rerun months or years later, sometimes by new teams.

With this new landscape, the how and why of AIRR data analysis are evolving:

  • The focus is moving from "can I parse my data?" to "can I robustly extract insights, find biomarkers, and build ML-ready features for discovery or diagnostics?"

  • It's not enough for a toolkit to just work. It needs to scale, interoperate, and empower new kinds of science, including complex Deep Learning and foundation models.

By taking a step back and rethinking the core "how" and "why" of AIRR analysis, immunarch prepares you for the next epoch of immunomics -- so your science is ready, whatever comes next.

[!WARNING] immunarch is evolving towards 1.0 version and undergoing huge changes. Please check the updates here: https://github.com/immunomind/immunarch/issues/432

To install the legacy 0.9.1 release, use pak::pak("immunomind/immunarch@0.9.1"). Its API reference and tutorials are available in the 0.9.1 documentation archive.

To install the latest 1.0 pre-release version, use pak::pak("immunomind/immunarch")

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before installing any release or pre-release version of immunarch, please install pak that will simplify the installation of any package, not just immunarch:

install.packages("pak", repos = sprintf("https://r-lib.github.io/p/pak/stable/%s/%s/%s", .Platform$pkgType, R.Version()$os, R.Version()$arch))

More info if needed is available on pak website.

docs.title: Install the latest version
docs.text:
To install the latest release of immunarch, simply run:

pak::pak("immunomind/immunarch")

Mind that this will install the package from our GitHub instead of CRAN. This method is much preferred due to limitations of CRAN and reliance on other packages, which are distributed via pak as well.

docs.title: ⚡ Quick Start
docs.text:
# Install `pak` - a blazingly-fast package manager
install.packages("pak", repos = sprintf("https://r-lib.github.io/p/pak/stable/%s/%s/%s", .Platform$pkgType, R.Version()$os, R.Version()$arch))

# Install and load immunarch along with the pre-packaged data
pak::pak("immunomind/immunarch")
library(immunarch)
immdata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")

# Calculate and plot core AIRR statistics
airr_desc_genes(immdata, gene_col = "v_call") |> vis()
repsim_jaccard(immdata) |> vis()
airr_diversity_pielou(immdata) |> vis()
airr_diversity_chao1(immdata) |> vis()
airr_clonality_prop(immdata)

# Read bulk AIRR files listed in the manifest's file column
manifest <- read_manifest("data/manifest.csv")
immdata <- read_repertoires(
  "<manifest>", schema = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"),
  manifest = manifest, count_col = "counts"
)

# Or specify the input files directly
immdata <- read_repertoires(
  "data/*.tsv.gz", schema = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"),
  manifest = manifest, count_col = "counts"
)

Oh, and one small thing. Even if you have tens of gigabytes of the data, you won't need to adapt the code to a server. The code will be exactly the same — immunarch got your back thanks to immundata.

# Note: this command is the same

# Repertoire similarity - overlap, Jaccard, Morisita-Horn

docs.title: 🪲 Bugs and Issues
docs.text:
The mission of immunarch is to make bulk and single-cell immune repertoires analysis painless. All bug reports, documentation improvements, enhancements and ideas are appreciated. Just let us know via GitHub (preferably) or support@immunomind.com (in case of private data).

Bug reports must:

  1. Include a short, self-contained R snippet reproducing the problem.
  2. Add a minimal data sample for us to reproduce the problem. In case of sensitive data you can send it to support@immunomind.com instead of GitHub issues.
  3. Explain why the current behavior is wrong/not desired and what you expect instead.
  4. If the issue is about visualisations, attach a picture to help us reproduce the bug.

We are always open to contributions. There are three ways to contribute:

  1. Create an issue here and describe what would you like to improve or discuss.

  2. Create an issue or find one here, fork the repository and make a pull request with the bugfix or improvement.

  3. Find an existing issue and help others resolve this.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Retired the v0 API. Legacy calls now stop with a deprecation error. Use immunarch 0.11.x to run v0 scripts. Migration guide
  • Removed data.table, dtplyr, and other dependencies used only by v0.

docs.title: immunarch 0.11.0 (November 2026)
docs.text: This release adds receptor tracking, publicness analysis, sequence clustering, and basic immunoglobulin mutation analysis. It also expands repertoire similarity and adds rarefaction and extrapolation.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• Renamed airr_stats_chains(), airr_stats_genes(), and airr_stats_lengths() to airr_desc_chains(), airr_desc_genes(), and airr_desc_lengths().
  • Renamed airr_public_intersection() and airr_public_jaccard() to repsim_intersection() and repsim_jaccard().
  • If you used clust_cc() in an earlier development build, pass the contracted graph from dist_hamm(..., mode = "graph") as edges.

docs.title: New features and improvements
docs.text:
• Added vdj_track() to follow selected receptors across samples, time points, or tissues. Use output = "df" to get a table with zero counts for receptors absent from a repertoire. Plot the tracked abundances with vis().
  • Added annotate_public() to measure receptor incidence and abundance across repertoires and strata. Use vdj_public() and make_public_filter() to select receptors by incidence, count, or proportion. Use vis() to plot incidence distributions and public receptor selections.
  • Added dist_hamm() for grouped Hamming distances and clust_cc() for connected-component clustering. Distance calculations support thresholds, sampling within groups, and separate comparisons by locus for paired chains.
  • Added Chao-Jaccard, Morisita-Horn, and Bray-Curtis repertoire similarity. Shared-receptor counts and Jaccard similarity skip unshared receptors when building repertoire pairs. All five similarity methods support pairwise dot plots with vis().
  • Updated descriptive statistics for paired chains. Added vis() plots for chain counts and for rank-abundance, rank bins, and clonal space.

docs.title: Receptor annotation
docs.text:
• Added annotate_with_database() to attach a reference database label by matching selected receptor features.
  • Added annotate_ig_clones() to assign immunoglobulin clones from heavy-chain or paired-chain data. Use read_germline_references() to load IMGT references and annotate_ig_germlines() to reconstruct clone-level germlines.
  • Added annotate_ig_shm() to count replacement and silent mutations against aligned germlines. Use airr_ig_shm() to summarize mutation counts and frequencies by repertoire, with summaries across sequences and across clones.

docs.title: Rarefaction and extrapolation
docs.text:
• Added airr_diversity_rarefaction() and support for plotting its results with vis(). The function requires positive integer clonotype counts.
  • Interpolation uses the exact hypergeometric expectation for sampling without replacement. This corrects underestimated richness in earlier development builds.
  • Extrapolation uses the finite-sample Chao estimator and defaults to twice the observed sample size. Confidence bounds use an abundance-distribution bootstrap and both probabilities supplied through quantile.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed Chao1 richness estimates for repertoires with doubletons and no singletons. airr_diversity_dxx(..., perc = 100) now returns observed richness even when cumulative proportions round below 100%.
  • Repertoire similarity counts each receptor once per repertoire when calculating shared receptor counts or Chao-Jaccard abundances.
  • AIRR methods now honor options(immunarch.autojoin = FALSE) and avoid duplicating repertoire metadata columns already present in the output.
  • Fixed DuckDB 2.0 compatibility for Hamming distances, clone annotation, and somatic hypermutation annotation.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
• The January 2027 release, immunarch 0.12.0, will remove legacy functions that currently raise deprecation warnings. Run immunarch::get_immunarch_news() for migration help. Migration guide, single-cell tutorial
  • Include the warning and a small reproducible example when reporting a migration problem. GitHub issues

docs.title: Clonality - receptor overabundance statistics for immune repertoires
Description
docs.text:
A family of functions to quantify receptor overabundance per repertoire. It helps in deciphering the structure and partition the repertoire. Higher clonality means that one or several receptors are over-expanded. Such effects is usually associated with the ongoing immune system response or anomalous behaviour, e.g., in blood cancers.

Available functions

The following methods are available.

1) Rank-abundance lines (airr_clonality_line). Prepare a plot for each repertoire. It orders receptors from most to least abundant and keeps the top limit receptors. Use it to see whether a small number of receptors dominate the repertoire: a steep line suggests strong clonal expansion.

2) Rank-bin statistics (airr_clonality_rank). Summarise how much of a repertoire is occupied by receptors in different rank ranges. Receptors are ordered by proportion and grouped using rank thresholds such as the top 10, top 100, or top 1,000 receptors. Use it to compare whether expansion is concentrated in the highest-ranked receptors across repertoires.

3) Proportion-bin statistics (airr_clonality_prop). Summarise how much of a repertoire is occupied by receptors at different abundance levels. It assigns each receptor to a proportion-based group, such as "Hyperexpanded", "Large", or "Ultra-rare". Each bin contains receptors with the proportion in the specified limits – just like in a histogram. Use it to compare the balance of expanded and rare receptors across repertoires.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
airr_clonality_line(
  idata,
  limit = 1e+05,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_clonality_rank(
  idata,
  bins = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 10000, 1e+05),
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_clonality_prop(
  idata,
  bins = c(Hyperexpanded = 0.01, Large = 0.001, Medium = 1e-04, Small = 1e-05, Rare =
    1e-06),
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object. limit A single whole number greater than or equal to 10, giving the maximum number of top receptors to keep per repertoire (default 100000). autojoin Logical. If TRUE, join repertoire metadata by the schema repertoire id. Change the default behaviour by calling options(immunarch.autojoin = FALSE). format String. One of "long" ("long" tibble with imd_repertoire_id, facet columns, and value; useful for visualizations) or "wide" (wide/unmelted table of features, with each row corresponding to a specific repertoire / pair of repertoires; useful for Machine Learning). bins A named numeric vector of thresholds (e.g., c(Hyperexpanded = 1e-2, Large = 1e-3, ...)). Names become bin labels and must be non-empty. Internally sorted in descending order for assignment. Result rows follow the supplied bin order, with "Ultra-rare" last.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
1) Rank-abundance lines (airr_clonality_line)

A tibble with columns:

  • imd_repertoire_id - repertoire identifier
  • index - rank within repertoire (1 = most abundant)
  • imd_count - receptor count used for ranking
  • imd_proportion - receptor proportion within the repertoire
  • plus any repertoire metadata columns carried from idata\$repertoires
2) Rank-bin statistics (airr_clonality_rank)

A tibble with

  • repertoire_id
  • clonal_rank_bin - the rank threshold (e.g., 10, 100, ...)
  • occupied_prop - sum of proportion within the bin
  • plus repertoire metadata columns from idata\$repertoires
3) Proportion-bin statistics (airr_clonality_prop)

A tibble with

  • repertoire_id
  • clonal_prop_bin - factor-like label from names(bins) or "Ultra-rare"
  • occupied_prop - sum of proportion within the bin
  • plus repertoire metadata columns from idata\$repertoires

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
All three airr_clonality_*() results can be passed directly to vis(). With autojoin = TRUE (the default), repertoire metadata is included in the result and can be selected by the plotting arguments.

1) Rank-abundance lines (airr_clonality_line)

vis() plots receptor rank (index) against imd_proportion on a logarithmic y-axis by default. The line plot accepts:

  • yval selects either "imd_proportion" (the depth-normalised default) or "imd_count" (raw observed counts).
  • color colours the lines by a repertoire or metadata column. Lines remain grouped by repertoire when a metadata column is selected.
  • log = FALSE switches to a linear y-axis.
  • facet splits the plot by one column, or creates a facet grid when given two columns; dir = "h" or dir = "v" controls the wrapping direction.
  • title replaces the default plot title.
2) Rank-bin statistics (airr_clonality_rank)

vis() produces a stacked column plot of occupied_prop per repertoire, filled by clonal_rank_bin. Receptors beyond the largest requested rank have a missing bin and are not drawn, so the total bar height shows the repertoire space occupied by the displayed ranks.

vis() produces a stacked column plot of occupied_prop per repertoire, filled by clonal_prop_bin. The "Ultra-rare" bin is included, so each complete repertoire normally sums to 100%.

Both stacked plots accept xval, yval, and fill to remap columns, plus facet, dir, and title for layout and labeling.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A family of functions that summarise the basic structure of immune repertoires. These summaries help you check data quality, compare samples, and describe chain counts, sequence lengths, and gene usage before more detailed analyses.

Available functions

The following methods are available.

1) Chain counts (airr_desc_chains). Count V(D)J chains in each repertoire, optionally grouped by locus. Use this method to check capture depth, compare library sizes, examine TRA/TRB/IGH balance, and identify locus-specific loss or over-representation.

2) Sequence-length distribution (airr_desc_lengths). Count sequences of each length per repertoire, optionally grouped by annotation columns. Use this method to describe CDR3 length distributions, detect possible library preparation bias, compare groups, and create length-based features.

3) Gene usage (airr_desc_genes). Count V(D)J gene segments per repertoire, optionally grouped by locus. The method can count unique receptors or sum barcode/UMI counts. Use it to compare gene usage between groups, identify unusual gene patterns, and create repertoire-level features.

A tibble with columns:

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
All three airr_desc_*() results can be passed directly to vis(). With autojoin = TRUE (the default), repertoire summaries and user metadata are included in the result and can be selected by the plotting arguments.

1) Chain counts (airr_desc_chains)

vis() plots one point per repertoire, with n_barcodes on the x-axis and n_receptors on the y-axis. Both axes use log scales. Dashed lines mark overall receptor-to-barcode ratios of 100%, 50%, and 25%. Locus-specific rows share the same repertoire totals, so they appear as one point. The plot accepts:

  • label selects one or more columns for point labels; the default is imd_repertoire_id.
  • colour colours points by a repertoire metadata column. fill is accepted as an alias for existing calls.
  • title replaces the default plot title.

For single-cell data, n_barcodes is the observed cell count; for bulk data, it is total abundance. The ratio shows repertoire-level richness, not how many receptors occur within each barcode.

2) Sequence-length distribution (airr_desc_lengths)

vis() plots seq_len on the x-axis and prop on the y-axis, filled by repertoire. Set fill to a metadata or grouping column to compare groups with box-and-violin distributions. facet accepts one column for a wrapped layout or two columns for a facet grid; dir = "h" or dir = "v" controls the wrapping direction.

3) Gene usage (airr_desc_genes)

vis() produces a dot plot with gene segments as rows, repertoires as columns, and n mapped to dot size and colour. Use row to select the gene column, col to select repertoire or metadata columns, and value to select the numeric measure. size_max_mm controls the largest dot; row_order and col_order set the display order.

docs.title: Diversity - estimating the heterogeneity of immune repertoires
Description
docs.text:
A family of functions to quantify receptor diversity in each repertoire. Diversity describes how many different receptors are present and how evenly their abundances are distributed. These methods help you compare repertoire structure, detect clonal expansion, and assess sampling depth.

Available functions

The following methods are available.

1) Coverage diversity (airr_diversity_dxx). Calculate the minimum number of the most abundant receptors needed to cover perc% of a repertoire. For example, D50 is the number of receptors that cover half of the repertoire. Use it to identify repertoires dominated by expanded receptors.

2) Chao1 richness (airr_diversity_chao1). Estimate the total number of receptors, including receptors that may be missing because of limited sampling. Use this non-parametric estimator when rare receptors suggest that the observed repertoire is incomplete.

3) Rarefaction and extrapolation (airr_diversity_rarefaction). Estimate how receptor richness changes with sample size. Use interpolation to compare repertoires at a common sampling depth and extrapolation to estimate how many additional receptors may be found with deeper sampling.

Computation is done in RAM after one database query that fetches only the repertoire identifier and receptor counts. Interpolation uses the exact hypergeometric expectation for sampling without replacement. Extrapolation uses the finite-sample Chao estimator, and confidence bounds use bootstrap standard errors from an estimated abundance distribution. Clonotype counts must be positive integers.

4) Shannon entropy (airr_diversity_shannon). Calculate Shannon entropy from receptor proportions in each repertoire. The value increases when a repertoire contains more receptors or has a more even abundance distribution. Use it as one summary that reflects both richness and evenness.

5) Pielou evenness (airr_diversity_pielou). Calculate how evenly receptor abundance is distributed within each repertoire. The method divides Shannon entropy by the maximum entropy for the observed richness. Use it to compare evenness between repertoires with different numbers of receptors.

6) Diversity index (airr_diversity_index). Calculate the Hill number at q = 1, which is the exponential of Shannon entropy calculated with natural logarithms. Use it as an effective number of receptors that is easy to compare between repertoires.

7) Hill numbers (airr_diversity_hill). Calculate a diversity profile for one or more orders q. At q = 0, the result is receptor richness; at q = 1, it is the exponential of Shannon entropy; higher values of q give more weight to abundant receptors. Use several orders to compare the influence of rare and abundant receptors.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
airr_diversity_dxx(
  idata,
  perc = 50,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_chao1(
  idata,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_rarefaction(
  idata,
  step = NA,
  quantile = c(0.025, 0.975),
  extrapolation = NA,
  nboot = 50,
  norm = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_shannon(
  idata,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_pielou(
  idata,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_index(
  idata,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

airr_diversity_hill(
  idata,
  q = 0:5,
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object. perc A number or numeric vector in (0, 100] (default 50), e.g. 50 for D50, 20 for D20. autojoin Logical. If TRUE, join repertoire metadata by the schema repertoire id. Change the default behaviour by calling options(immunarch.autojoin = FALSE). format String. One of "long" ("long" tibble with imd_repertoire_id, facet columns, and value; useful for visualizations) or "wide" (wide/unmelted table of features, with each row corresponding to a specific repertoire / pair of repertoires; useful for Machine Learning). step A whole number greater than or equal to 1, or NA. The default, NA, uses up to 50 evenly spaced points through the smallest observed depth. Each repertoire gets up to 50 points for each remaining interpolation and extrapolation interval. quantile A numeric vector of length 2 containing confidence probabilities strictly between 0 and 1. extrapolation A nonnegative whole number or NA giving the upper size limit for extrapolation. Use 0 to disable extrapolation. The default, NA, uses twice each repertoire's observed clone count. nboot A nonnegative whole number that is either 0 or at least 2. It gives the number of bootstrap replicates used to estimate confidence bounds. Defaults to 50; use 0 to return NA confidence bounds. norm A single logical value; if TRUE, size is divided by total repertoire size and richness estimates are divided by observed richness. verbose A single logical value controlling whether a concise progress message is shown. q A numeric scalar or vector of nonnegative orders. Defaults to 0:5.

docs.text:
1) Coverage diversity (airr_diversity_dxx)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • perc
  • dxx - minimal count of top receptors to reach perc%
  • plus repertoire metadata from idata\$repertoires
2) Chao1 richness (airr_diversity_chao1)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • Estimator - estimated receptor richness
  • SD - standard deviation for the estimator value
  • Conf.95.lo - CI 0.025
  • Conf.95.hi - CI 0.975
  • plus repertoire metadata from idata\$repertoires
3) Rarefaction and extrapolation (airr_diversity_rarefaction)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • size - sample size (absolute or normalised)
  • q_low - lower confidence bound
  • mean - expected richness
  • q_high - upper confidence bound
  • type - interpolation or extrapolation
  • plus repertoire metadata from idata\$repertoires
4) Shannon entropy (airr_diversity_shannon)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • shannon - entropy in bits
5) Pielou evenness (airr_diversity_pielou)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • shannon
  • n_receptors
  • pielou - evenness in [0, 1] (NA if S <= 1)
6) Diversity index (airr_diversity_index)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • q = 1
  • hill_number
  • plus repertoire metadata from idata\$repertoires
7) Hill numbers (airr_diversity_hill)

A tibble with:

  • imd_repertoire_id
  • q - Hill order
  • hill_number - true diversity of order q
  • plus repertoire metadata from idata\$repertoires

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
Most airr_diversity_*() results can be passed directly to vis(). With autojoin = TRUE (the default), repertoire metadata is included in the result and can be selected by the plotting arguments.

1) Coverage diversity (airr_diversity_dxx)

vis() plots dxx for each repertoire. When several perc values are present, use fill = "perc" to show a separate column for each coverage threshold.

2) Chao1 richness (airr_diversity_chao1)

vis() produces a column plot of the estimated richness (Estimator) for each repertoire.

3) Rarefaction and extrapolation (airr_diversity_rarefaction)

vis() plots estimated richness (mean) against sample size (size). Use color to group curves, show_ci = FALSE to hide confidence intervals, and log = TRUE to use a logarithmic x-axis.

4) Shannon entropy (airr_diversity_shannon)

vis() produces a column plot of shannon for each repertoire.

5) Pielou evenness (airr_diversity_pielou)

vis() produces a column plot of pielou for each repertoire.

6) Diversity index (airr_diversity_index)

vis() produces a column plot of hill_number at q = 1 for each repertoire.

7) Hill numbers (airr_diversity_hill)

This result does not currently have a dedicated vis() method. Use the returned q and hill_number columns to create a diversity profile.

docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Summarize the mutation counts and frequencies produced by annotate_ig_shm(). Aggregation runs in DuckDB on the duckplyr-backed input.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
airr_ig_shm(
  idata,
  by = NA_character_,
  clone_col = "clone_id",
  autojoin = getOption(IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_OPTION, IMMUNARCH_AUTOJOIN_DEFAULT),
  format = c("long", "wide")
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object with SHM annotations and clones. by Character vector, NA, or NULL. The default uses the canonical locus column when available. Use NULL to pool loci. Repertoires are always summarized separately; clone IDs cannot be included in by. clone_col Column containing clone assignments. Missing clone IDs are included in sequence summaries but excluded from clone summaries. autojoin Logical. If TRUE, join repertoire metadata by the schema repertoire id. Change the default behaviour by calling options(immunarch.autojoin = FALSE). format Inherited from the common AIRR interface. This method always returns long-format summaries.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
This function uses the mutation counts and frequencies already calculated by annotate_ig_shm(). Here, a sequence means one immunoglobulin chain sequence in the input.

The function summarizes these counts and frequencies in two ways:

  • Across sequences: each sequence has equal weight. A clone with more sequences therefore contributes more to the result.
  • Across clones: first calculate a mean or median within each clone, then summarize these clone means or medians. Each clone has equal weight, regardless of how many sequences it contains.

These calculations do not use read counts or UMI counts as weights.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: A long-format table of repertoire statistics. Each row contains the repertoire ID, any by columns, region, mutation, measure, and the 24 statistics listed above. Repertoire metadata is added by default.

docs.title: Output statistics
docs.text:
Each repertoire has several output rows. The columns region, mutation, and measure tell you which mutation counts or frequencies the row describes:

Column Meaning region The region being analyzed: overall for all available annotated regions; v for FWR1 through FWR3; cdr for all available CDRs; fwr for all available framework regions; or one region such as cdr3. mutation replacement for mutations that change the amino acid, silent for mutations that do not change the amino acid, or total for replacement plus silent mutations. See annotate_ig_shm() for counting rules. measure count for the number of mutations, or freq for mutation frequency. Frequencies are fractions: 0.05 means 5%.

The other columns contain the statistics for that row. For example, consider four sequences in one repertoire. Clone A has total CDR3 mutation counts of 0, 0, and 9. Clone B has one sequence with 6 total CDR3 mutations. Part of the output would be:

imd_repertoire_id region mutation measure sequence_mean clone_mean_mean clone_median_mean 1 cdr3 total count 3.75 4.5 3

All three statistics in this row describe total CDR3 mutation counts:

  • sequence_mean: average the four counts: (0 + 0 + 9 + 6) / 4 = 3.75.
  • clone_mean_mean: the clone means are 3 and 6. Their mean is 4.5.
  • clone_median_mean: the clone medians are 0 and 6. Their mean is 3.

A row with measure = "freq" contains the same kinds of statistics for mutation frequencies instead of mutation counts. Results are calculated separately for each repertoire and each group selected with by, such as locus. Repertoire metadata is added when autojoin = TRUE.

The full list of 24 statistics is below. In every description, the mutation count or frequency is the one specified by region, mutation, and measure in that row. q25 and q75 are the lower and upper quartiles (25th and 75th percentiles).

Column Meaning n_sequences Number of input sequences, including those with a missing mutation count or frequency, or a missing clone ID. n_valid Number of sequences with an available mutation count or frequency. n_missing Number of sequences whose mutation count or frequency is NA: n_sequences - n_valid. n_valid_without_clone Number of sequences with an available mutation count or frequency but no clone ID. n_zero Number of sequences with a mutation count or frequency of zero. zero_prop Proportion of sequences with zero mutations of this type in this region, among sequences with an available count or frequency: n_zero / n_valid. sequence_mean Mean mutation count or frequency across sequences. Each sequence has equal weight. sequence_median Median mutation count or frequency across sequences. sequence_q25 Lower quartile of mutation counts or frequencies across sequences. sequence_q75 Upper quartile of mutation counts or frequencies across sequences. n_clones Number of clones with a known clone ID, including clones for which all mutation counts or frequencies are missing. n_valid_clones Number of clones with at least one sequence whose mutation count or frequency is available. n_valid_with_clone Number of sequences with both an available mutation count or frequency and a clone ID. clone_mean_weighted_mean Mean mutation count or frequency across sequences with a clone ID. This is also the mean of clone means weighted by the number of sequences with available counts or frequencies in each clone. clone_mean_mean Calculate the mean mutation count or frequency in each clone, then take the mean of these clone means. Each clone has equal weight. clone_mean_median Calculate the mean mutation count or frequency in each clone, then take the median of these clone means. clone_mean_q25 Lower quartile of the clone means. clone_mean_q75 Upper quartile of the clone means. clone_median_mean Calculate the median mutation count or frequency in each clone, then take the mean of these clone medians. Each clone has equal weight. clone_median_median Calculate the median mutation count or frequency in each clone, then take the median of these clone medians. clone_median_q25 Lower quartile of the clone medians. clone_median_q75 Upper quartile of the clone medians. n_zero_clone_means Number of clones whose mean mutation count or frequency is zero. n_zero_clone_medians Number of clones whose median mutation count or frequency is zero.

Missing mutation counts or frequencies (NA) are excluded from means, medians, quartiles, and the denominator of zero_prop. Zero is included. Sequences without clone IDs are included in sequence statistics but excluded from clone statistics. Clones with no available mutation counts or frequencies are included in n_clones but excluded from the clone means, medians, and quartiles. If none of the required counts or frequencies are available, the mean, median, quartiles, and zero_prop are NA. Quartiles use linear interpolation.

Combined region frequencies come from annotate_ig_shm(), which divides the total mutation count by the total number of comparable bases in those regions. This function does not average the frequencies of different regions to obtain a combined frequency. Regions without the required input columns are skipped.

docs.title: Annotate clonality - per-receptor labels for overabundance
Description
docs.text:
A small family of helpers that add clonality labels to each receptor in an immundata::ImmunData object.

Available functions
  • annotate_clonality_rank() - label by rank bins within each repertoire.
  • annotate_clonality_prop() - label by proportion bins (named thresholds).

annotate_clonality_rank() - for each repertoire, receptors are ordered by within-repertoire abundance (proportion) and assigned a rank bin label.

annotate_clonality_prop() - label each receptor by proportion bin using named thresholds (matched in descending order; else "Ultra-rare").

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
annotate_clonality_rank(idata, bins = c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 10000, 1e+05))

annotate_clonality_prop(
  idata,
  bins = c(Hyperexpanded = 0.01, Large = 0.001, Medium = 1e-04, Small = 1e-05, Rare =
    1e-06)
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object. bins A named numeric vector of thresholds (e.g., c(Hyperexpanded = 1e-2, Large = 1e-3, ...)). Names become bin labels and must be non-empty. Internally sorted in descending order for assignment. Result rows follow the supplied bin order, with "Ultra-rare" last.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
An immundata::ImmunData whose $annotations gains:

  • clonal_rank_bin - integer-like label with the applied rank threshold (outside all thresholds -> NA).

An immundata::ImmunData whose $annotations gains:

  • clonal_prop_bin - label from names(bins) or "Ultra-rare".

docs.text:
• Per-repertoire summaries: airr_clonality
  • Data container: immundata::ImmunData

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")

idata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")
idata_rank <- annotate_clonality_rank(idata)
idata_prop <- annotate_clonality_prop(idata)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A family of functions for analysing and adding biologically useful immunoglobulin annotations to receptors. These annotations help connect receptor sequence variation with clonal expansion and B-cell evolution.

Each function has its own dedicated help page, so click on the function names to open corresponding pages.

Available functions
  1. Clonal family inference (annotate_ig_clones()). Usually the very first step in any of the Ig analysis workflows. The function clusters Ig receptors to clonal families using heavy-chain or paired heavy-light junction similarity by Hamming distance.
  2. Germline annotation (annotate_ig_germlines()). The first step in the somatic hypermutation (SHM) analysis workflows. This function annotates the Ig receptors with information about germline genes for the subsequent SHM analysis.
  3. Somatic hypermutation computation (annotate_ig_shm()). The second and the final step in the SHM analysis workflows. This function computes the SHM per-receptor and aggregated statistics and annotates the receptors with them. After that you can use airr_ig_shm() to explore and analyse the repertoire-wide and family-wide statistics in a more convenient form.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: annotate_ig_clones(), annotate_ig_germlines(), annotate_ig_shm()

docs.title: Build and annotate immunoglobulin clonal families
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Build clonal families from B-cell receptors and assign them to receptors.

Receptors are compared within a subject or repertoire. A heavy-chain edge requires a shared V/J union group, equal junction length, and normalized junction Hamming distance at or below heavy_threshold. Paired mode independently builds the corresponding light-chain graph and keeps receptors together only when they share both heavy- and light-chain families.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
annotate_ig_clones(
  idata,
  heavy_threshold,
  light_threshold = NULL,
  mode = c("auto", "heavy", "paired"),
  by_scope = "<auto>",
  junction_col = "junction",
  v_col = "v_call",
  j_col = "j_call",
  heavy_locus = "IGH",
  clone_col = "clone_id"
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata immundata::ImmunData. Paired or heavy-chain IG receptor data. heavy_threshold, light_threshold Numeric scalar or data frame. Normalized Hamming-distance threshold strictly between 0 and 1, or a complete table containing the by_scope column and a numeric threshold column. light_threshold defaults to heavy_threshold. mode Character scalar. Annotation strategy: "heavy" uses only the heavy chain, "paired" combines independently inferred heavy- and light-chain families, and "auto" selects paired mode for a paired IG receptor schema and heavy mode otherwise. by_scope Character scalar. Column that prevents clonal families from crossing biological subjects or repertoires. "<auto>" uses the first available subject-like column and otherwise the repertoire identifier. junction_col, v_col, j_col Character scalar. Columns containing the nucleotide junction, V call, and J call. V and J calls are grouped at gene level, allowing overlapping ambiguous assignments. heavy_locus Character scalar. Value identifying the heavy-chain locus. The default is "IGH"; all other loci declared by the receptor schema are treated as light chains in paired mode. clone_col Character scalar. Name of the combined clone annotation. The default is "clone_id".

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Connected components use single linkage: when A connects to B and B connects to C, all three receptors belong to one chain family even if A and C are farther apart than the threshold. Hamming distance compares only junctions of equal length, so it does not represent insertions or deletions.

Junction nucleotides are converted to uppercase. Junctions containing characters other than A, C, G, and T cannot create edges and remain isolated.

For grouping, V/J calls are split on commas or |, whitespace and allele suffixes are removed, and duplicate calls are ignored. Calls sharing both a V candidate and a J candidate are connected transitively within each scope and locus, before splitting by junction length or applying distance thresholds. Missing or empty gene calls cannot connect groups. Original calls and receptor IDs are preserved. The second example separately shows preprocessing when normalized calls should also define receptor identity.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: immundata::ImmunData. The original rows and columns plus clone_id (or the name supplied through clone_col), heavy_family_id, and light_family_id. Both chain rows of a paired receptor receive the same labels. In heavy mode, clone_id equals heavy_family_id and light_family_id is missing.

docs.title: Reconstruct clone-level immunoglobulin germlines
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
B cells in the same clone come from one starting cell, but their antibody sequences can gain different mutations over time. To study these mutations, we need a shared sequence to compare them with.

The method annotates each clone and locus with a representative germline sequence from references – usually IMGT germline table.

The result can be used as the reference for somatic hypermutation analysis with annotate_ig_shm().

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
annotate_ig_germlines(
  idata,
  references,
  species = NULL,
  by = "<auto>",
  sequence_id_col = "sequence_id",
  sequence_col = "sequence_alignment",
  v_col = "v_call",
  j_col = "j_call",
  v_start_col = "v_germline_start",
  v_end_col = "v_germline_end",
  j_start_col = "j_germline_start",
  j_end_col = "j_germline_end",
  germline_col = "germline_alignment"
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata immundata::ImmunData. AIRR data to annotate. references A table returned by read_germline_references() containing IMGT-gapped reconstruction references. These are not the ungapped reference files used to build an IgBLAST database; see Assumptions and reference compatibility. species Character scalar, or NULL to use the sole reference species. by Character vector or "<auto>". Clone grouping columns. Automatic grouping uses clone_id, with subject_id when available. Locus is always added. sequence_id_col, sequence_col, v_col, j_col Character scalars selecting the sequence ID, IMGT-gapped aligned sequence, V-call, and J-call columns. v_start_col, v_end_col, j_start_col, j_end_col Character scalars selecting the closed, IMGT-gapped germline-coordinate columns. germline_col Character scalar naming the reconstructed output column.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: immundata::ImmunData with one clone/locus germline assigned to each input row. Groups which cannot be reconstructed receive NA.

docs.title: Assumptions and reference compatibility
docs.text:
This function reconstructs germlines by indexing directly into the supplied reference strings. It does not insert IMGT numbering gaps, convert coordinates, or otherwise align the input sequences and references. Consequently, all of the following assumptions must hold:

  • sequence_col contains IMGT-gapped alignments, including the standard . numbering spacers.
  • The germline start and end columns use the same IMGT-gapped coordinate system as sequence_col and references.
  • V references in references contain IMGT numbering gaps. In particular, do not supply the ungapped FASTA files used to build an IgBLAST database.
  • The reference alleles and release match those used during assignment of the V and J calls. Missing or different alleles cannot be reconstructed safely.

An Immcantation-style workflow normally maintains two representations of the same reference release: ungapped sequences for the IgBLAST database and IMGT-gapped sequences for germline reconstruction. This function requires the latter. Matching references therefore means the same allele set and release, not the literal ungapped FASTA passed to IgBLAST.

read_germline_references() preserves gaps that are already present in a FASTA file, but neither it nor this function converts ungapped references to IMGT-gapped references. Supplying incompatible ungapped data can produce a plausible-length but incorrectly shifted germline without an error.

The reconstructed value corresponds conceptually to Dowser's germline_alignment_d_mask: the retained V and J portions surround an N-masked middle region. This function does not reconstruct a full V(D)J germline or infer a D segment.

docs.title: Preparing the input
docs.text:
To create the BCR repertoire, first you need to run IgBlast either standalone or through immundapter::tool_igblast() with an IMGT database on your FASTQ files or 10XGenomics contigs files. immundapter automatically prepares the alignment and V positions for IMGT-gapped references. Then, read V and J references from the same IMGT release with read_germline_references(). See the "Ig tutorial" on the website for the detailed workflow – it is a bit complicated, as per usual with BCR analysis.

Other AIRR data can be used when its alignment and V/J positions match the supplied IMGT-gapped references. But please mind that raw IgBlast AIRR output has not been prepared this way. This function does not convert positions or add gaps, so mismatched input can give an incorrect sequence without an error.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: This is a D-masked germline, not a complete ancestral receptor sequence. By default, it replaces an existing germline_alignment column. Use germline_col to keep that column.

docs.title: Annotate immunoglobulin somatic hypermutation
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Calculate overall, V-region, and AIRR-region somatic-hypermutation counts and frequencies from aligned observed and reconstructed germline sequences.

The input must contain the columns selected by sequence_col and germline_col, v_sequence_start, v_alignment_start, and the canonical AIRR *_start and *_end columns for FWR1, CDR1, FWR2, CDR2, FWR3, CDR3, and FWR4. The default germline column is normally created with annotate_ig_germlines().

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
annotate_ig_shm(
  idata,
  sequence_col = "sequence_alignment",
  germline_col = "germline_alignment",
  by = "<auto>"
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata immundata::ImmunData. IgBLAST AIRR data to annotate. sequence_col Character scalar. Aligned observed-sequence column. germline_col Character scalar. Aligned reconstructed germline column. sequence_col and germline_col may select alternative alignment columns, but those columns must use the same alignment and coordinate system as the canonical AIRR region-coordinate columns. by Character vector, "<auto>", or NULL. Columns used to calculate group-level mu_freq summaries. The default uses clone_id, with subject_id when available; locus is added when available. NULL skips grouped summaries.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
AIRR region coordinates are interpreted as 1-based closed intervals on the unaligned query sequence. v_alignment_start identifies the aligned position corresponding to v_sequence_start. While mapping query positions, N consumes a query coordinate, whereas . and - do not.

A position is comparable only when both aligned characters are unambiguous A, C, G, or T nucleotides. Thus N, ., and - positions contribute to neither mutation counts nor frequency denominators. mu_count is the sum of classifiable replacement and silent mutations across all available regions; mu_freq divides that count by the number of comparable positions in those regions. Overall and combined CDR/FWR replacement and silent frequencies use the sum of comparable positions across their selected regions, not aggregated regional frequencies. Individual-region frequencies use the comparable positions in that region as their denominator.

Replacement and silent consequences are classified independently for each mutation against the germline codon. Stop-producing substitutions are not counted as either class. If one boundary of a region is missing, all four outputs for that region are missing while other regions and overall outputs remain available. A valid region with no comparable positions has zero counts and missing frequencies. Combined CDR and framework metrics use the available regions in their respective sets. If no region in a set has both boundaries, all combined outputs for that set are missing.

When grouping is enabled, mu_freq_median and mu_freq_mean summarize non-missing mu_freq values without weighting, and mu_freq_n counts their contributors. Rows missing any grouping key receive missing median and mean values and a zero count. Explicit by columns are used exactly as supplied; include locus explicitly to keep heavy and light chains separate. Use dplyr::distinct() on the grouping columns and summaries when a group-level rather than row-level result is needed.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: immundata::ImmunData. The input rows with combined mu_count and mu_freq columns plus replacement and silent counts and frequencies overall, across the V region (FWR1 through FWR3), across all CDRs, across all framework regions, and for each individual region. When grouping is enabled, the result also includes mu_freq_median, mu_freq_mean, and mu_freq_n on every row.

docs.title: Why SHM results may differ between tools
docs.text: Results can differ between SHM tools, even for the same sequences. This function counts a mutation only when its codon (a group of three bases) is complete and has no alignment gap. Other tools may count mutations in codons with gaps. Removing . characters from an IMGT alignment can also shift codon boundaries and change which mutations are counted, including mutations that create a stop codon. For a fair comparison, use matching alignments and region positions, and check how each tool handles gaps and stop codons.

A family of functions for clustering sparse receptor graphs represented by an ImmunData object and an immunarch_sequence_graph.

clust_cc() finds receptor-level connected components from the contracted sequence graph returned by dist_hamm() with mode = "graph".

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
clust_cc(
  idata,
  edges,
  by = NULL,
  cluster_col = "cluster_id",
  size_col = "cluster_size"
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object. Its receptor annotations provide the graph nodes through the canonical receptor-ID column and, when requested, repertoire metadata. edges An immunarch_sequence_graph returned by dist_hamm() with mode = "graph". Ordinary receptor edge tables are not accepted. by A character vector of column names or NULL. These columns come from the receptor annotations in idata; each distinct combination is an independent clustering scope. The scope may be broader than the comparison groups used by dist_hamm(). The canonical receptor-ID column cannot also be used in by. cluster_col A single character string giving the output component-identifier column name. Within each by group, the identifier is the minimum original receptor identifier in that component. Defaults to "cluster_id". size_col A single character string giving the output component-size column name. The size is the number of distinct original receptors in the component. Defaults to "cluster_size".

docs.title: Details
docs.text: Sequence-node distances are applied only where both nodes participate in the same clustering scope. If one receptor belongs to several sequence nodes in a scope, those nodes are joined by identity edges before components are computed. Receptors without a usable sequence remain singleton components.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
A lazy duckplyr table with one row per distinct, non-missing receptor ID per clustering scope and the following columns:

  • the grouping columns supplied through by, in the same order;
  • the canonical receptor identifier;
  • the component identifier, named by cluster_col; and
  • the number of distinct receptors in that component, named by size_col.

Call dplyr::collect() when an in-memory tibble is needed.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A family of functions to calculate sequence distances between immune receptors. These methods help you explore receptor similarity, select thresholds for Immunoglobulin clone assignment, and construct sparse receptor-similarity graphs.

Available functions

The following methods are available.

1) Hamming distances (dist_hamm). Compute an upper-triangular sparse edge table of Hamming distances between receptor IDs represented in the receptor annotations in idata. Comparisons are restricted to equal sequence lengths and equal values of by. The data are not grouped by repertoire automatically. For paired-chain receptor schemas, the canonical locus column is added to by automatically, so distances are computed separately per locus. Add it explicitly if you have a non-AIRR-C standard locus column name.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
dist_hamm(
  idata,
  seq_col = "cdr3_aa",
  by = NULL,
  max_dist = NULL,
  min_sim = NULL,
  sample_n = 0L,
  sample_by = "<auto>",
  mode = c("pairs", "graph")
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object. seq_col A single character string naming a sequence feature in the receptor schema. by A character vector or NULL. These optional annotation columns must be equal within a receptor pair. For B-cell clone assignment, a typical choice is c("v_call", "j_call"); add imd_repertoire_id when comparisons must stay within repertoires, or subject_id if your data has such a dedicated column for subject-specific metadata. Locus grouping is also always applied for paired-chain receptor schemas. max_dist A single nonnegative number, a keyed threshold table, or NULL. Scalar values in (0, 1) bound normalized Hamming distance; integer values which are >=1 bound raw Hamming distance. NULL (the default) and the legacy scalar value 0 disable bounding. A threshold table must contain one or more key columns plus a numeric threshold column strictly inside (0, 1). Its key columns must be included in by and must exactly cover the corresponding input key combinations. Mutually exclusive with min_sim. min_sim A single number in [0, 1] or NULL, giving the minimum normalized Hamming similarity. It is mutually exclusive with max_dist. sample_n A nonnegative whole number giving the maximum number of distinct receptor IDs to sample before distance calculation within each sample_by group. 0 (the default) disables sampling. sample_by A single character string or NULL selecting the column to sample by. The default, "<auto>", uses the first available column among subject_id, donor, donor_id, patient_id, patient, subject, and imd_repertoire_id. The resolved column must also be supplied through by. Set to NULL to sample from the whole dataset without accounting for groups. This argument is ignored when sample_n = 0. mode Output representation. "pairs" (the default) returns the receptor-pair table described below. "graph" returns contracted sequence-node edges and receptor-to-node membership. Grouping columns cannot use names reserved for structural columns in the selected output.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
1) Hamming distances (dist_hamm)

With mode = "pairs", a lazy duckplyr table with:

  • grouping columns supplied through by
  • locus for paired-chain receptor schemas
  • imd_receptor_id_1, imd_receptor_id_2 – canonical receptor identifiers, with imd_receptor_id_1 < imd_receptor_id_2
  • seq_len
  • dist – raw Hamming distance
  • norm_dist – dist / seq_len
  • sim – normalized Hamming similarity, 1 - norm_dist

With mode = "graph", an immunarch_sequence_graph object containing two lazy duckplyr tables. edges contains the effective grouping columns, globally unique from and to node IDs, and seq_len, dist, norm_dist, and sim. membership contains the effective grouping columns, the canonical receptor ID, and node_id. A receptor can have multiple membership rows, and membership includes nodes without edges. Nodes represent distinct combinations of the full effective comparison group and a non-missing, non-empty sequence; sequences themselves are not returned.

Call dplyr::collect() only when a returned table is small enough for memory.

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
Distance results can be passed directly to vis().

1) Hamming distances (dist_hamm)

vis() plots the normalized distance to the nearest non-identical neighbor for each receptor by default. This is the distribution used for manual IG clone-threshold selection. When a subject column can be inferred using the same priority as sample_by = "<auto>", one panel is drawn per subject; otherwise, a single pooled distribution is drawn.

Use mode = "all" to plot every pairwise distance instead of nearest neighbors. Pass one of the following values to xval to change what will be plotted: "norm_dist" (the default), "dist" (non-normalised distnaces), or "sim" (similarity). Set facet = NULL to have one plot per all input samples, or name a result column to facet by it. binwidth and title customize the histogram.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: immundata::ImmunData

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")


idata <- get_test_idata()


# Build the computing query
res <- dist_hamm(idata)
# Check how results would look like
res
# Run the computation query and upload the results to the memory
res <- res |> collect()

# Bound Hamming distance.
# Non-normalised -- no receptors with more than 1 mismatch in the output
res <- dist_hamm(idata, max_dist = 1) |> collect()
res


# Normalised -- no receptors with more than .2 normalised distance in the output
res <- dist_hamm(idata, max_dist = .2) |> collect()
res

# Similarity, inverse to normalised distance -- no receptors with
# less than 0.9 similarity in the output
# The results are the same as for the previous normalised run
res <- dist_hamm(idata, min_sim = .8) |> collect()
res

# Plot normalized nearest-non-identical-neighbor distances.
vis(dist_hamm(idata))
# Plot all raw pairwise distances instead.
vis(dist_hamm(idata), mode = "all", xval = "dist")

#
# Typical use case for BCR data
#

# BCR-style V/J/length blocking with at most three mismatches, inside patients
clone_edges <- dist_hamm(
  idata_bcr,
  seq_col = "junction",
  by = c("patient", "v_call", "j_call"),
  max_dist = 3
)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A family of functions to compare shared receptors between repertoires. These methods help you measure repertoire similarity, identify public receptors, compare biological groups, and check whether replicate samples have similar receptor composition.

Available functions

The following methods are available.

1) Shared-receptor counts (repsim_intersection). Count the unique receptors shared by each pair of repertoires. Use this method to find related samples, check replicate similarity, or identify receptors shared across many repertoires.

2) Jaccard similarity (repsim_jaccard). Compare the sets of unique receptors in each pair of repertoires. The score accounts for the total number of unique receptors in both repertoires. Use it to compare receptor overlap when repertoire sizes differ.

$J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}$ 3) Chao-Jaccard similarity (repsim_chao_jaccard). Compare receptor overlap using receptor counts. The method estimates similarity after allowing for shared receptors that may be missing because one or both repertoires were sampled at limited depth. Use it when sampling depth may affect the observed overlap. 4) Morisita-Horn similarity (repsim_morisita_horn). Compare receptor abundance profiles. Abundant receptors have more influence on the score than rare receptors. Use it to determine whether the same expanded receptors dominate two repertoires. The method uses imd_proportion as the abundance measure.

C\_{MH} = {(\_i + \_j) N_i N_j} 5) Bray-Curtis similarity (repsim_bray). Measure how similar two receptor abundance profiles are. This is one minus Bray-Curtis dissimilarity: 0 means no overlap, and 1 means identical abundance composition. The method uses imd_proportion as the abundance measure. Set transform = "log1p" to reduce the influence of the most abundant receptors and give lower-abundance receptors more influence on the result. This can reveal broader repertoire similarity when a few expanded receptors would otherwise dominate the comparison. The transformation is applied inside the database query and does not modify idata. Immune-repertoire studies commonly calculate Bray-Curtis measures from clonotype proportions without an additional transformation. Therefore, transform = "none" remains the default. The "log1p" option is an exploratory sensitivity analysis based on a common ecological pre-treatment for reducing the effect of dominant taxa. After transformation, the values no longer sum to one, and the result no longer has the simple interpretation of the fraction of original repertoire abundance that overlaps. ## Usage 

repsim_intersection(idata)

repsim_jaccard(idata)

repsim_chao_jaccard(idata)

repsim_morisita_horn(idata)

repsim_bray(idata, transform = c("none", "log1p"))
## Arguments idata An immundata::ImmunData object. transform A single character string selecting the transformation applied to imd_proportion before calculating similarity. Use "none" (the default) for the original proportions or "log1p" for log(1 + imd_proportion).

S_{BC,ij} = 1 - \frac{\sum_k |a_{ik} - a_{jk}|} {\sum_k (a_{ik} + a_{jk})} = \frac{2\sum_k \min(a_{ik}, a_{jk})}{\sum_k (a_{ik} + a_{jk})} where $a_{ik}$ is the original or transformed abundance of receptor $k$ in repertoire $i$.

## Value 1) Shared-receptor counts (repsim_intersection) A symmetric numeric matrix where rows/columns are repertoire labels derived from schema_repertoire. Each cell is the count of shared unique receptors. The diagonal contains per-repertoire richness (total unique receptors). 2) Jaccard similarity (repsim_jaccard) A symmetric numeric matrix where rows/columns are repertoire labels derived from schema_repertoire. Each cell is the Jaccard similarity in \[0, 1\]. The diagonal is 1. 3) Chao-Jaccard similarity (repsim_chao_jaccard) A symmetric numeric matrix where rows/columns are repertoire labels derived from schema_repertoire. Each cell is the Chao-Jaccard similarity in \[0, 1\] (1 = maximum estimated overlap, 0 = no observed shared receptors). The diagonal is 1. 4) Morisita-Horn similarity (repsim_morisita_horn) A symmetric numeric matrix whose rows/columns are repertoire labels derived from schema_repertoire, with values in \[0, 1\] (0 = no shared abundance, 1 = identical abundance composition). The diagonal is 1. Comparisons involving an empty repertoire are NA. 5) Bray-Curtis similarity (repsim_bray) A symmetric numeric matrix where rows/columns are repertoire labels derived from schema_repertoire. Each cell is Bray-Curtis similarity in \[0, 1\] (0 = no overlap, 1 = identical). The diagonal is 1. ## Visualisation All five repsim\_\*() results can be passed directly to vis(). vis() displays the result as a dot plot, with repertoire labels on both axes. Each dot represents one pair of repertoires; its size and fill show the value for that pair. 1) Shared-receptor counts (repsim_intersection) Larger and brighter dots mean that the repertoires share more unique receptors. The matrix diagonal contains repertoire richness; the plot omits self-comparisons. 2) Jaccard similarity (repsim_jaccard) Larger and brighter dots mean greater similarity between the sets of unique receptors. Values range from 0 (no shared receptors) to 1 (identical receptor sets). 3) Chao-Jaccard similarity (repsim_chao_jaccard) Larger and brighter dots mean greater estimated similarity after correction for receptors that may be missing because of limited sampling. Values range from 0 (no observed shared receptors) to 1 (maximum estimated similarity). 4) Morisita-Horn similarity (repsim_morisita_horn) Larger and brighter dots mean greater similarity between receptor abundance profiles. Values range from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical abundance composition). 5) Bray-Curtis similarity (repsim_bray) Larger and brighter dots mean greater similarity between receptor abundance profiles. Values range from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical abundance composition). All plots omit self-comparisons. Their color legends mark the smallest, midpoint, and largest plotted pairwise values. All repertoire-similarity plots accept:
  • size_max_mm to set the maximum dot diameter.
  • row_order and col_order to set the repertoire order on each axis.
