docs.title: Select receptors by their incidence across repertoires or strata
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text: Select shared receptors, receptors private to a strata, or receptors absent above an abundance threshold. Define one or more rules to select receptors by their sharing and abundance in comparison populations using make_public_filter().

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: vdj_public(idata, ..., output = c("immundata", "df"))

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object with defined repertoires. ... One or more rules created by make_public_filter(). With no rules, require presence in at least two input repertoires. output A character scalar: "immundata" returns a new ImmunData, "df" returns a data frame convenient to immediately pass to vis().

docs.title: Details
docs.text: Input counts and proportions are saved as imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion. The input is unchanged. No per-rule incidence columns or custom attributes are added.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: A new ImmunData or collected observation table.

docs.title: Repeated calls
docs.text: Warning: Applying vdj_public() to an already filtered result overwrites imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion with abundances from its immediate input. Since proportions are recalculated after filtering, the saved proportions no longer refer to the repertoire before the first call. Keep the original ImmunData as a reference when calculating percentages relative to the original repertoires. To apply several rules to the same original input, pass them together in one vdj_public() call.

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
Plot the selected receptors with vis(selected, plot = "public", reference = idata), where idata is the original input to vdj_public(). Alternatively, pipe vdj_public(idata, output = "df") to vis(reference = idata); its result class selects this plot automatically. The ordinary observation rows in the collected output are unchanged.

Bars show abundance, the sum of the selected identities' saved original repertoire proportions, read against the left percentage axis. Dots show coverage, the number of selected identities detected in each repertoire, read against the right receptor-count axis. Dot labels give the detected/selected counts; bar labels give abundance percentages. Observed occurrences below selection thresholds still contribute to both measures. Coverage describes the selected set, not the fraction of all receptor identities in a repertoire. Individual receptor trajectories can be visualised with vdj_track().

The required reference defines the complete input repertoire population, retaining repertoires with no selected receptors at zero. Use the selected result and its own original reference: repertoire metadata is matched using the reference repertoire schema because filtering can rebuild repertoire IDs. The reference does not restore abundances overwritten by repeated vdj_public() calls; the saved original proportions must refer to this baseline. An empty selection cannot be plotted.

xval selects a repertoire ID or metadata column for the x-axis; each value must identify one repertoire. fill selects a repertoire metadata column for colour and defaults to the defined strata when available. Repertoires are ordered by colour group and x value; factor levels control their order. title changes the title or removes it with NULL.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text: make_public_filter(), annotate_public()

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")

idata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")

# Keep receptors shared across at least two repertoires.
shared <- vdj_public(idata)
shared$repertoires

#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   imd_repertoire_id Therapy n_barcodes n_receptors
#>               <int> <chr>        <dbl>       <int>
#> 1                 1 CAR-T          124          70
#> 2                 2 ICI            122          70

vis(shared, plot = "public", reference = idata)

# Work with repertoire and strata rules.
idata <- get_test_idata() |>
  agg_repertoires(c("Response", "Therapy")) |>
  agg_strata("Therapy")

vdj_public(idata, output = "df") |>
  vis(reference = idata, fill = "Therapy")

# Inspect strata and find the IDs for the two therapies.
groups <- idata$strata
groups

#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   imd_strata_id strata_name Therapy
#>           <int> <chr>       <chr>  
#> 1             1 Strata1     CAR-T  
#> 2             2 Strata2     ICI

ici <- groups$imd_strata_id[groups$Therapy == "ICI"]
car_t <- groups$imd_strata_id[groups$Therapy == "CAR-T"]

# The test data has one repertoire per therapy, so use incidence >= 1.
in_ici <- vdj_public(idata, make_public_filter(
  strata = ici, min_incidence = 1L
))

# Count distinct strata instead of repertoires.
across_therapies <- vdj_public(idata, make_public_filter(
  incidence_by = "strata", min_incidence = 2L
))

# Present in ICI and absent in CAR-T. Collect the retained observations.
ici_only <- vdj_public(
  idata,
  make_public_filter(strata = ici, min_incidence = 1L),
  make_public_filter(strata = car_t, max_incidence = 0L),
  output = "df"
)
ici_only |>
  dplyr::select(
    cdr3_aa, v_call, Therapy, imd_orig_count,
    imd_orig_proportion
  ) |>
  head()

#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   cdr3_aa       v_call     Therapy imd_orig_count imd_orig_proportion
#>   <chr>         <chr>      <chr>            <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 ASFPVLSPYNEQF TRBV28*01  ICI                  1             0.00105
#> 2 ASRAGAGTGELF  TRBV19*01  ICI                  1             0.00105
#> 3 ASRWGTEAF     TRBV19*01  ICI                  1             0.00105
#> 4 ASRLGPNNEQF   TRBV7-2*01 ICI                  1             0.00105
#> 5 ASSYSEGVIYGYT TRBV6-5*01 ICI                  1             0.00105
#> 6 ASSYGPQEGYT   TRBV6-5*01 ICI                  1             0.00105

# Select by repertoire IDs and require count >= 5 in an ICI repertoire.
ids <- idata$repertoires |>
  dplyr::filter(Therapy == "ICI") |>
  dplyr::pull(imd_repertoire_id)
abundant <- vdj_public(idata, make_public_filter(
  repertoires = ids, min_count = 5
))
# All observations of passing receptors are retained throughout idata.

docs.title: Track selected immune receptors across time and space
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Use vdj_track() to follow receptors across samples, time points, tissues, or cell populations. For example, select abundant receptors before treatment and find their abundances in later samples. You can also follow a set of sequences identified in another experiment.

Select receptors with the argument from, or use n to select the most abundant receptors in each source repertoire. Follow them throughout the target idata, including repertoires where they are rare or unobserved. The input ImmunData object is not changed.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: vdj_track(idata, from = NULL, n = NULL, output = c("immundata", "df"))

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: idata An immundata::ImmunData object with defined repertoires. These are the repertoires through which receptors will be followed. from NULL, a numeric vector of repertoire IDs, an immundata::ImmunData object, or a data frame. NULL, the default, uses every target repertoire as a source. Numeric values select source imd_repertoire_id values in idata. An ImmunData source supplies its observed receptor identities. A data frame supplies exact column combinations to match, such as junction alone or junction together with v_call. Tibbles and duckplyr tables are also accepted. tibble::tibble is recommended. n A non-negative whole number or NULL. Select up to n receptors with the highest counts in each source repertoire, then follow their combined set of identities. Equal counts are resolved by receptor ID, as in immundata::top_n(). NULL, the default, selects all source receptors. This argument applies only when from is NULL or contains repertoire IDs. output A character scalar. "immundata", the default, returns a new ImmunData object containing the selected receptors' observed cells and chains. "df" returns an abundance-summary tibble with one row per selected receptor and input repertoire, including explicit zeros where unobserved. Both outputs preserve the original target abundances. The summary retains input receptor and repertoire IDs, receptor identity features, and repertoire metadata as columns, and ready for plotting with vis().

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
An ImmunData source must use the same receptor features and chain schema as the target. Complete feature combinations, including both chains of a paired receptor, are matched

Column names same as in the idata must exist in the target observations in the from argument. Matching is exact and case-sensitive, with no sequence or gene-call normalization. Missing query values in from are not allowed. Unmatched queries, empty query tables, and n = 0 produce an empty result.

docs.title: Value
docs.text:
With output = "immundata", a new immundata::ImmunData object containing the selected receptors' observed rows, with imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion.

With output = "df", an immunarch result tibble containing:

  • imd_receptor_id and receptor identity features from the input receptor dictionary. Paired-chain features are shown side by side.
  • imd_receptor_label, a readable label combining the receptor features. Paired-chain labels include both loci and use + between chains.
  • imd_repertoire_id and metadata from the input repertoire table.
  • imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion, including zeros where the receptor was unobserved. Proportions use the original repertoire totals.

Each selected receptor has exactly one row in every input repertoire. Receptor features sharing a name with repertoire metadata receive the suffix _receptor. Barcode, chain-observation, and other row-level fields are excluded. The tibble is recognised by vis() and needs no attached repertoire metadata. Empty selections produce a zero-row summary with the same column structure.

docs.title: Common use cases
docs.text:
• Follow receptors from one or several samples. Supply their repertoire IDs through from. Receptors are followed in every target repertoire, including those outside the source selection.
  • Follow the top receptors from one sample. Supply a repertoire ID and n, for example from = 5L, n = 3L for the top three from repertoire ID 5.
  • Follow the top receptors from every sample. Supply n and leave from = NULL. A receptor selected in any source is followed everywhere, even where it is below the top n. The combined set can contain more than n identities.
  • Follow an upstream selection. Pass an ImmunData object containing receptors of interest, such as expanded clones or a selected cell population. The source can also come from an independent import.
  • Follow a sequence panel. Pass a table containing sequences and optional gene or locus columns. All columns in a row must match the same chain; rows are alternatives. Matching one chain keeps the complete receptor, including its partner for paired receptors.

docs.title: Original abundances
docs.text:
imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion columns in the output store the target receptors counts and proportions before vdj_track filters the data. Use these columns to compare abundances across the original samples. The ordinary imd_count and imd_proportion describe the filtered object, following normal immundata behavior, i.e., normalising the proportions. Please be careful - another vdj_track call replaces the original-abundance columns imd_orig_count and imd_orig_proportion.

The ImmunData result contains observed chains only and follows normal immundata filtering, including rebuilding IDs for the remaining repertoires. In other words, the repertoire ID could change after calling vdj_track with output = "immundata". This is temporary inconvenience, sorry for that. The good news is that no repertoire metadata is missing so you still analyse the data. The "df" summary uses the input IDs and contains zero-count rows for unobserved combinations. These are abundance rows, without barcode or observation-specific fields. A receptor not observed in a sample is not necessarily biologically absent.

docs.title: Visualisation
docs.text:
Pass vdj_track(..., output = "df") directly to vis(). The summary tibble carries a result class that selects the tracking plot. The default ImmunData output is intended for further analysis, so pass output = "df" whenever you want to plot the results.

vis() draws an alluvial plot of imd_orig_proportion by imd_repertoire_id by default. Receptors are distinguished by colour and labelled by their receptor features in the legend, for example AAA V01. For paired receptors, each chain's locus and features are combined, for example IGH AAA V01 + IGL BBB V02. Receptor IDs remain the grouping keys, so pairs sharing one chain remain separate trajectories. The plot accepts:

  • plot = "alluvial" (the default) draws stacked bars connected by smooth ribbons and requires the optional package ggalluvial.
  • plot = "area" draws stacked areas.
  • plot = "line" draws individual trajectories with points.
  • xval selects the repertoire ID or metadata column for the x-axis. The default is to use the numeric repertoire IDs. This allows you to select metadata columns such as "Timepoint".
  • yval selects "imd_orig_proportion" (the default) or "imd_orig_count". These preserve abundances from the original target repertoires. Proportions are not renormalised to the selected receptors and need not sum to 100%.
  • facet selects one metadata column for separate panels. Each x value within a panel must identify exactly one repertoire. Define repertoires upstream to pool samples; plotting does not aggregate them.
  • title replaces the default title, "Receptor tracking".

The summary already contains zero abundances for unobserved receptor-repertoire combinations. Every original target repertoire remains on the plot, including samples with no tracked observations.

Repertoire metadata is returned in regular columns for every target sample, including samples with no tracked observations. Use those columns for xval and facet, or prepare additional display columns in the summary.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• vis() for plotting the tracking abundance summary.
  • immundata::top_n() for selecting abundant receptors upstream.
  • immundata::filter_immundata() for filtering observations upstream.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")

library(immundata)

# A small bulk dataset sampled at four time points.
# At T3, only TTT is observed; neither AAA nor CCC is observed.
rows <- tibble::tibble(
  sample = c(rep(c("T0", "T1", "T2"), each = 3), "T3"),
  junction = c(
    "AAA", "CCC", "GGG", "AAA", "CCC", "TTT",
    "AAA", "GGG", "ACG", "TTT"
  ),
  v_call = c("V1", "V2", "V1", "V1", "V2", "V3", "V1", "V1", "V4", "V3"),
  abundance = c(8L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 9L, 4L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 5L)
)
input <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
readr::write_tsv(rows, input)
idata <- read_repertoires(
  input,
  schema = c("junction", "v_call"), count_col = "abundance",
  repertoire_schema = "sample", output_folder = tempfile("vdj-track-"),
  preprocess = NULL, postprocess = NULL, rename_columns = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE
)
source_id <- idata$repertoires |>
  dplyr::filter(sample == "T0") |>
  dplyr::pull(imd_repertoire_id)

# Follow every receptor observed at T0, or only its two most abundant ones.
from_t0 <- vdj_track(idata, from = source_id)


top_from_t0 <- vdj_track(idata, from = source_id, n = 2L)

# Follow any receptor that is the most abundant in at least one repertoire.
top_from_each <- vdj_track(idata, n = 1L)

# An upstream selection can also supply the receptors to follow.
selected <- immundata::top_n(idata, n = 1L)
from_selected <- vdj_track(idata, from = selected)

# Match sequences alone, or exact sequence/gene combinations.
from_sequences <- vdj_track(idata, from = tibble::tibble(
  junction = c("AAA", "GGG")
))
from_panel <- vdj_track(idata, from = tibble::tibble(
  junction = c("AAA", "CCC"), v_call = c("V1", "V2")
), output = "df")

# The summary already has one row per receptor and repertoire: 2 x 4 rows.
from_panel

#> # A tibble: 8 × 10
#>   imd_receptor_id junction v_call imd_receptor_label imd_repertoire_id sample
#> *           <int> <chr>    <chr>  <chr>                          <int> <chr> 
#> 1               3 CCC      V2     CCC V2                             1 T0    
#> 2               4 AAA      V1     AAA V1                             1 T0    
#> 3               3 CCC      V2     CCC V2                             2 T1    
#> 4               4 AAA      V1     AAA V1                             2 T1    
#> 5               3 CCC      V2     CCC V2                             3 T2    
#> 6               4 AAA      V1     AAA V1                             3 T2    
#> 7               3 CCC      V2     CCC V2                             4 T3    
#> 8               4 AAA      V1     AAA V1                             4 T3    
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: n_barcodes <int>, n_receptors <int>,
#> #   imd_orig_count <dbl>, imd_orig_proportion <dbl>

# Both selected receptors have explicit zero counts and proportions at T3.
from_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(sample == "T3") |>
  dplyr::select(sample, junction, imd_orig_count, imd_orig_proportion)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   sample junction imd_orig_count imd_orig_proportion
#>   <chr>  <chr>             <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1 T3     CCC                   0                   0
#> 2 T3     AAA                   0                   0

# Select baseline receptors, then visualise their original abundances.
tracked <- vdj_track(idata, from = source_id, n = 2L, output = "df")
tracked$sample <- factor(tracked$sample, levels = c("T0", "T1", "T2", "T3"))
# T3 remains on each plot, with both receptor abundances at zero.
# Legend labels combine receptor features automatically, for example AAA V1.
vis(tracked, xval = "sample")

vis(tracked, xval = "sample", plot = "area")

vis(tracked, xval = "sample", plot = "line")

# Plot original counts instead of proportions.
vis(tracked, xval = "sample", plot = "line", yval = "imd_orig_count")

docs.title: Visualise public receptor selection, incidence, or pairwise frequencies
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Visualise selected receptor coverage and abundance with plot = "public", or receptor frequencies shared between two repertoires with the default plot = "pairwise". For annotate_public() results, plot = "incidence" shows receptor counts by the number of repertoires in which they occur.

In pairwise plots, receptor proportions are shown on log-scaled axes. Point fill shows the log proportion ratio between the x and y repertoires.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
## S3 method for class 'ImmunData'
vis(
  .data,
  x = 1,
  y = 2,
  density = TRUE,
  lm = TRUE,
  plot = c("pairwise", "public", "incidence"),
  reference = NULL,
  xval = "imd_repertoire_id",
  fill = NULL,
  title = "Selected immune receptors across repertoires",
  ...
)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: .data An immundata::ImmunData object with aggregated repertoires. x Repertoire for the x-axis. Either a numeric repertoire index, repertoire ID, or a repertoire schema value. y Repertoire for the y-axis. Either a numeric repertoire index, repertoire ID, or a repertoire schema value. density Logical. If TRUE, show marginal distributions of unique and public receptor proportions. lm Logical. If TRUE, add a linear model fit and adjusted R-squared. plot One of "pairwise" (the default), "public", or "incidence". reference For plot = "public", the original ImmunData supplied to vdj_public(). It defines the complete repertoire axis, including repertoires without selected receptors. Required for this plot. xval For plot = "public", the repertoire ID or metadata column used for x-axis labels. Each value must identify one repertoire. fill For plot = "public", a repertoire metadata column used for colour. NULL uses strata_name when strata are defined; otherwise the plot uses a single colour. title For plot = "public" or "incidence", the plot title, or NULL to omit it. Each view has its own default title. ... Must be empty.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: The incidence view stacks within-stratum receptor counts when strata are defined. An identity observed in several strata contributes once to each stratum's distribution; stack totals are not globally distinct receptor counts. Without strata, one unstacked global distribution is shown and every identity contributes once. This view uses statistics from the last annotate_public() call; rerun annotation after changing the population. Both publicness views use vertical legends on the right and wrap long colour labels for display without changing the underlying names.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: A ggplot2 or patchwork object.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")

idata |> vis()
idata |> vis(x = 1, y = 2)
idata |> vis(x = "Blood", y = "Tumor")
idata |> vis(x = 1, y = 2, density = FALSE)
selected <- vdj_public(idata)
vis(selected, plot = "public", reference = idata)
annotate_public(idata) |> vis(plot = "incidence")

docs.title: One function to visualise them all
docs.text: Source code

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
vis() is a lightweight, quick-look plotting helper. It's designed to help you visualise results fast with sensible defaults. It automatically detects the input type and chooses an appropriate visualisation (e.g., output from airr_desc_genes() is recognised as gene usage values and plotted without extra arguments).

vis() is not intended for publication-quality figures. For serious, highly customised, or publication-ready plots, I recommend building your graphics directly with ggplot2.

Information on how visualise a specific result from a domain, e.g., clonality or diversity, is available at each domain's help page in the visualisation section. Take a look at the "See also" section down below to see links to the domains, which support visualisations.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: vis(.data, ...)

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: .data The output from any immunarch analysis function. The function automatically resolves to a correct visualisation. ... Any other arguments, see the "Details" section for specific visualisation functions.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
vis() chooses a plot based on the analysis result. Start with vis(result), then consult the documentation for the analysis that created it to see its plotting defaults and supported arguments.

E.g., for clonality results, see airr_clonality by running ?airr_clonality. Or see repsim For repertoire similarity by running ?repsim.

docs.title: Value
docs.text: A ggplot2 object.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• airr_desc for descriptive statistics visualisations.
  • airr_clonality for clonality visualisations.
  • airr_diversity for diversity visualisations.
  • repsim for repertoire similarity visualisations.
  • dist for receptor distance visualisations.
  • vdj_track for receptor tracking visualisations with output = "df".
  • vdj_public for selected receptor coverage and abundance. Pass its output = "df" result and the original reference to vis(), or use plot = "public" for its ImmunData result.
  • annotate_public for incidence distributions with plot = "incidence", stacked by stratum when strata are defined and unstacked otherwise.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
library("immunarch")

immdata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")
airr_desc_genes(immdata, gene_col = "v_call") |> vis()
repsim_jaccard(immdata) |> vis()
airr_diversity_pielou(immdata) |> vis()
airr_diversity_chao1(immdata) |> vis()
# Tracking summaries include explicit zeros for unobserved combinations.
vdj_track(immdata, n = 5, output = "df") |> vis()
vdj_public(immdata, output = "df") |> vis(reference = immdata)
annotate_public(immdata) |> vis(plot = "incidence")

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
This reference covers the current immunarch v1 API.

  • Describe repertoires with airr_desc, airr_clonality, and airr_diversity.
  • Compare repertoires with repsim and find shared receptors with vdj_public.
  • Track receptors across samples with vdj_track.
  • Annotate receptors with annotate_clonality, annotate_with_database, and annotate_ig_clones.
  • Calculate sequence distances with dist and cluster sequences with clust.

The retired v0 API page lists functions from the legacy API. The internal helpers im_common_args and register_immunarch_method have been retired.

For tutorials, see the single-cell guide and migration guide. The frozen immunarch 0.9.1 archive covers the old release.

docs.title: 🧬 immunarch – Multi-modal immune repertoire analysis in R
docs.text:
immunarch brings a comprehensive analytics toolkit to build reproducible analysis pipelines for Adaptive Immune Receptor Repertoire (AIRR) data with a particular focus on designing personalized immunotherapies and vaccines. Key features are:

  • Multi-modal immune profiling: compute receptor- and repertoire-level statistics leveraging single-cell, spatial, immunogenicity or any other receptor annotations;

  • Immunomics at scale: work seamlessly with datasets that don’t fit in memory;

  • Immune biomarker discovery: stratify cohorts and timepoints, derive repertoire signatures (diversity/clonality, V/J usage, similarity), and track antigen-annotated clonotypes;

  • Feature engineering: build Machine Learning-ready feature tables (receptor-, sample- and cohort-level) from core repertoire metrics and annotations, with consistent IDs/metadata for downstream statistics or modeling;

  • Modular, extendable, adaptable: add new analyses and metrics via an extension API, and use adapters to interoperate with other AIRR tools and formats.

docs.title: 🤔 Why immunarch?
docs.text:
As immune repertoire sequencing becomes a mainstream technology, adopted by major platforms and integrated into more translational and clinical workflows, tooling expectations are changing rapidly. The pace of innovation and data growth sometimes outstrips what even the most dedicated tool developers can deliver.

That’s why it’s the perfect moment to step back and rethink how and why we analyze AIRR data. Instead of racing to patch each new problem, we need to prepare for the next epoch of immunomics.

What defines this next epoch?

A massive shift in focus: from pure research towards biomarker discovery, personalized immunotherapies, and integration of immune repertoire data into real clinical decision-making.

Today’s AIRR analysis must handle:

  • Multi-modal data: bulk and single-cell V(D)J, spatial transcriptomics, gene expression, clinical metadata, and antigen specificity – all together;

  • Massive scale: experiments that move from gigabytes to tens or hundreds of gigabytes, or even terabytes;

  • Reproducibility and collaboration: workflows that need to be shared, versioned, and rerun months or years later, sometimes by new teams.

With this new landscape, the how and why of AIRR data analysis are evolving:

  • The focus is moving from “can I parse my data?” to “can I robustly extract insights, find biomarkers, and build ML-ready features for discovery or diagnostics?”

  • It’s not enough for a toolkit to just work. It needs to scale, interoperate, and empower new kinds of science, including complex Deep Learning and foundation models.

By taking a step back and rethinking the core “how” and “why” of AIRR analysis, immunarch prepares you for the next epoch of immunomics – so your science is ready, whatever comes next.

docs.title: ⚡ Quick Start
docs.text:
# Install `pak` - a blazingly-fast package manager
install.packages("pak", repos = sprintf("https://r-lib.github.io/p/pak/stable/%s/%s/%s", .Platform$pkgType, R.Version()$os, R.Version()$arch))

# Install and load immunarch along with the pre-packaged data
pak::pak("immunomind/immunarch")
library(immunarch)
immdata <- get_test_idata() |> agg_repertoires("Therapy")

# Calculate core AIRR statistics
airr_desc_genes(immdata, gene_col = "v_call")
repsim_jaccard(immdata)
airr_clonality_prop(immdata)
airr_diversity_pielou(immdata)

# Read bulk AIRR files listed in the manifest's file column
manifest <- read_manifest("data/manifest.csv")
immdata <- read_repertoires(
  "<manifest>", schema = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"),
  manifest = manifest, count_col = "counts"
)

# Or specify the input files directly
immdata <- read_repertoires(
  "data/*.tsv.gz", schema = c("cdr3_aa", "v_call"),
  manifest = manifest, count_col = "counts"
)

Oh, and one small thing. Even if you have tens of gigabytes of the data, you won’t need to adapt the code to a server. The code will be exactly the same — immunarch got your back thanks to immundata.

docs.title: 🪲 Bugs and Issues
docs.text:
The mission of immunarch is to make bulk and single-cell immune repertoires analysis painless. All bug reports, documentation improvements, enhancements and ideas are appreciated. Just let us know via GitHub (preferably) or support@immunomind.com (in case of private data).

Bug reports must:

  1. Include a short, self-contained R snippet reproducing the problem.
  2. Add a minimal data sample for us to reproduce the problem. In case of sensitive data you can send it to support@immunomind.com instead of GitHub issues.
  3. Explain why the current behavior is wrong/not desired and what you expect instead.
  4. If the issue is about visualisations, attach a picture to help us reproduce the bug.

We are always open to contributions. There are three ways to contribute:

  1. Create an issue here and describe what would you like to improve or discuss.

  2. Create an issue or find one here, fork the repository and make a pull request with the bugfix or improvement.

  3. Find an existing issue and help others resolve this.

docs.title: Limit the number of threads used by immunarch
What is happening under the hood?
docs.text:
immunarch uses immundata, which uses duckplyr, which runs queries in DuckDB. It is quite a journey from the data to your plots.

DuckDB can use many CPU cores by default to run faster, but sometimes you want to limit this.

docs.title: Why limit threads?
docs.text:
• On shared machines (servers, CI), many threads can slow down other users.
  • In tutorials, fewer threads make examples more predictable and easier to reproduce.
  • Lower threads = lower CPU load (but slower queries).

docs.title: How to limit the number of threads
docs.text:
Put this near the start of your tutorial/script:

# Limit the number of CPU threads used by DuckDB in this R session
duckplyr::db_exec("SET threads TO 1")

Change later (example: use 4 threads) or reset to default:

duckplyr::db_exec("SET threads TO 4")   # use 4 threads
# or, if supported in your environment:
duckplyr::db_exec("RESET threads")      # back to DuckDB default
